extracted.intended_audience: students of mathematical logic / readers learning first-order semantics
extracted.subtask_description: Definitions, propositions and exercises giving the standard Tarskian semantics for first-order logic: structures, variable assignments, values of terms, satisfaction clauses, and basic semantic notions (validity, entailment, satisfiability).

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure for a language (Definition 71A)
rubrics_metrics.description: A structure A for a language L consists of: (1) a non-empty domain |A|; (2) for each constant symbol c of L, an element c^A ∈ |A|; (3) for each n-place predicate symbol R (other than =) an n-place relation R^A ⊆ |A|^n; (4) for each n-place function symbol f, an n-place function f^A : |A|^n → |A|.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the standard specification of what it means to 'interpret' the non-logical vocabulary of a first-order language. The textbook emphasizes the non-empty domain stipulation and gives examples (e.g. structures for arithmetic and set theory). It also notes terminological variants: 'structure', 'interpretation', or 'model'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-empty domain and its consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: The domain of a structure must be non-empty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text explains consequences of forbidding empty domains: e.g. given the usual semantics for quantifiers, ∃x (α(x) ∨ ¬α(x)) becomes valid, and requiring constants to denote something in the domain ensures existential generalization (α(a) ⇒ ∃x α(x)) is sound. Allowing empty domains or non-denoting names leads toward 'free logic' and changes these inference patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of closed terms (Definition 72A)
rubrics_metrics.description: If t is a closed term in language L and A is a structure for L, then the value t^A is defined: (1) if t is a constant symbol c, then t^A = c^A; (2) if t ≡ f t1 ... tn then t^A = f^A(t1^A, ..., tn^A).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives the inductive computation of the denotation of closed terms using the functions and constants assigned by the structure. Illustrated by numeric examples in arithmetic-like languages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Covered structure (Definition 72B)
rubrics_metrics.description: A structure is covered iff every element of the domain is the value of some closed term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a language with constant symbols zero, one, two, ... yields a covered structure if the domain elements are exactly the values of those constants. The concept is used to discuss naming of domain elements by terms; not all structures are covered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variable assignment (Definition 73A)
rubrics_metrics.description: A variable assignment s for a structure A is a function s : Var → |A| mapping each variable to an element of the domain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Variable assignments supply values for variables that structures alone do not provide. They play a central role in defining the value of non-closed terms and satisfaction of formulas with free variables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of terms relative to assignment (Definition 73B)
rubrics_metrics.description: If t is a term, A a structure, and s a variable assignment, the value ¯s(t) is: (1) if t ≡ c then ¯s(t) = c^A; (2) if t ≡ x then ¯s(t) = s(x); (3) if t ≡ f t1 ... tn then ¯s(t) = f^A(¯s(t1), ..., ¯s(tn)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This inductive clause shows how to compute the denotation of arbitrary terms using both the structure and the variable assignment. The distinction between closed-term values (structure-only) and general-term values (assignment-dependent) is emphasized.

rubrics_metrics.name: x-variant and assignment update s[m/x] (Definitions 73C, 73D)
rubrics_metrics.description: An x-variant of s is any variable assignment s' that differs from s at most in what it assigns to x. For m ∈ |A|, the assignment s[m/x] maps x to m and agrees with s on all other variables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These notions are key for the semantics of quantifiers: satisfaction of quantified formulas is phrased in terms of checking the formula under x-variants that assign different domain elements to x.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satisfaction in a structure relative to an assignment (Definition 73E)
rubrics_metrics.description: The satisfaction relation |=_A α [s] is defined inductively: (1) Rt1...tn: iff ⟨¯s(t1),...,¯s(tn)⟩ ∈ R^A; (2) t1 = t2: iff ¯s(t1) = ¯s(t2); (3) ¬β: iff not |=_A β [s]; (4) (β → γ): iff not |=_A β [s] or |=_A γ [s]; (5) ∀x β: iff for every m ∈ |A|, |=_A β [s[m/x]].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The clauses show how atomic formulas, logical connectives and quantifiers are evaluated. Existential quantification is handled via ¬∀¬. The text explains why variable assignments are needed (terms like β(m) are not wffs) and gives worked examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existential satisfaction (derived clause)
rubrics_metrics.description: A wff ∃x α(x) is satisfied in A relative to s iff there exists m ∈ |A| such that |=_A α(x) [s[m/x]].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The textbook treats existential quantification as definable from universal and negation (∃x α ≡ ¬∀x ¬α) and provides worked examples showing how to check existence by searching assignments that witness the formula.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependence only on relevant variable assignments (Propositions 74A and 74B)
rubrics_metrics.description: If two assignments s1 and s2 agree on the variables occurring in a term t, then ¯s1(t) = ¯s2(t) (Prop 74A). If s1 and s2 agree on all free variables of α, then |=_A α [s1] iff |=_A α [s2] (Prop 74B).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These results formalize the idea that values and satisfaction only depend on assignments to the variables that actually occur. The text includes induction proofs and uses them to justify simplifying hypotheses about assignments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment-independence for sentences (Corollary 74C and Definition 74D)
rubrics_metrics.description: If α is a sentence (no free variables) then whether α is satisfied in A is independent of the variable assignment; |=_A α iff |=_A α [s] for every assignment s. Define |=_A α to mean |=_A α [s] for all s.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This justifies suppressing the assignment parameter when discussing truth of sentences in a structure. It is used to define satisfaction of sets of sentences and to talk about models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extensionality (Proposition 75A and Corollary 75B)
rubrics_metrics.description: If A1 and A2 have the same domain and, for every constant, relation, and function symbol occurring in α, their interpretations agree (c^{A1}=c^{A2}, R^{A1}=R^{A2}, f^{A1}=f^{A2}), then |=_{A1} α [s] iff |=_{A2} α [s]. For sentences, |=_{A1} α iff |=_{A2} α.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extensionality (relevance) says satisfaction depends only on the size of the domain and the interpretations of symbols that actually occur in the formula. The proof proceeds by induction on terms and formulas. This is useful for model-comparison arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substitution/value interaction (Propositions 75C and 75D)
rubrics_metrics.description: 75C: For term t and t', ¯s(t[t'/x]) = ¯_{s[¯s(t')/x]}(t). 75D: For wff α and term t', |=_A α[t'/x] [s] iff |=_A α [s[¯s(t')/x]].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These propositions allow either performing syntactic substitution first or computing the value of the substituting term and updating the assignment; both procedures yield the same result. They justify standard substitution/manipulation rules used in semantic proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions of basic semantic notions (Definitions 76A–76C)
rubrics_metrics.description: Validity: a sentence α is valid (⊨ α) iff |=_A α for every structure A. Entailment: Γ ⊨ α iff for every structure A, if |=_A Γ then |=_A α. Satisfiability: Γ is satisfiable iff there exists a structure A with |=_A Γ; otherwise Γ is unsatisfiable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These core notions relate truth-in-all-models, model-theoretic consequence, and the existence of models. The text gives standard logical relationships among them and uses them to formulate semantic metatheorems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence: validity and entailment by arbitrary Γ (Proposition 76D)
rubrics_metrics.description: A sentence α is valid iff Γ ⊨ α for every set of sentences Γ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: If α valid then trivially entailed by any Γ. Conversely, if α not valid there is a structure falsifying it; taking Γ = {⊤} shows there exists Γ that does not entail α. This exhibits the relationship between validity and universal entailment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entailment <-> unsatisfiability (Proposition 76E)
rubrics_metrics.description: Γ ⊨ α iff Γ ∪ {¬α} is unsatisfiable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard reduction: entailment fails exactly when there is a model of Γ making ¬α true; conversely, if Γ ∪ {¬α} is unsatisfiable then every model of Γ makes α true.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monotonicity of entailment (Proposition 76F)
rubrics_metrics.description: If Γ ⊆ Γ' and Γ ⊨ α then Γ' ⊨ α.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adding assumptions cannot remove consequences; shown by straightforward model-theoretic argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Semantic Deduction Theorem (Theorem 76G)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the semantic analogue of the syntactic deduction theorem: moving an assumption into the antecedent of an implication corresponds to changing entailment contexts. The proof is model-theoretic and given in the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universal instantiation (Proposition 76H)
rubrics_metrics.description: For wff α(x) and closed term t, ∀x α(x) ⊨ α(t).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a structure satisfies ∀x α(x) then, picking the assignment that maps x to t^A, one gets α(t) true in the structure. The text outlines this argument and refers to preceding substitution propositions.
